review_text: Casting aside my overwhelming disinterest in the subject, I can admit that Prof. Fletcher is a solid lecturer. Yet some reviewers have overlooked the flaws in his pedagogy, the exam policy, and the lopsided grading scheme. On one hand, he explains vital concepts, diagrams, and terms in an intelligible manner; on the other, he jams so much content into each session that recording notes by hand is not feasible. There are two options in this course: you can either bring a device to class or watch Panopto uploads after the fact. I can only speak for myself when I say that his quantity-over-depth approach has swayed me in favor of the latter. There is no point in attending class other than contributing to group assignments. While you receive many chances to succeed on exams (there are four in total), the other tasks barely nudge your grade in either direction, and rather than lessening the weight of your poorest exam score, he discards your worst concept check/group activity/SimuText scores instead, underscoring the fact that exams hold a staggering influence over grade calculation in this class. There is no exam curving, and you are also forbidden from using notes when taking exams. If students must be penalized, then it should be for a lack of understanding. It is quite different when students fail to recall one among countless testable pieces of information while three other courses are battling for room in their long-term storage. This unscientific closed-book policy is not specific to BSCI170, but I have to attack it whenever I see it. I neither recommend nor advise against taking this class--the positives and negatives level out. Do what you feel.
evidence_snippet: Yet some reviewers have overlooked the flaws in his pedagogy, the exam policy, and the lopsided grading scheme.

review_text: One of the easier upper level CS courses in that the material isn't conceptually demanding (compared to some of the low-level or mathy upper level CS courses). A better title for this course is "Mobile App Development" ("Programming Handheld Systems" can be misleading for embedded systems folks), and Dr. Franceschi uses Kotlin/Android Studio (as opposed to Flutter or React Native). Hence, a big part of doing well in the course is to familiarize yourself with Kotlin syntax and Android Studio, which he provides plenty of resources for. What you learn is relevant to mobile app development in general, regardless of the language/framework that's used in class. Syntax is the first thing you learn when picking up a new language, often followed by learning to read documentation. Writers of some of the other reviews seemed to miss this. If you're reading the other reviews for this course that complain about "unfair/pointless" grading, lack of a cheatsheet, points taken off for incorrect code logic, or other easily solvable concerns – keep in mind that in any course that emphasizes learning a new language or framework, you are tested on your knowledge of the language/framework, NOT how well you can use an IDE or autocomplete. If you're proficient in ANY object-oriented programming language, then you know the learning curve is steepest at the start. Stay up-to-date with the material for the first 1-2 weeks, and you'll quickly learn what approach works best for you with regards to grasping the material As for the class/grading structure, this is how it was for Fall 2025 (you can decide what's a pro or a con): - Dr. Franceschi posted all code and slides from class, and recorded every lecture to watch - in decreasing order of what was weighted most: final exam, total project grade, midterm, group project, quizzes. I understand the annoyance with quizzes because they could consist of questions from a range of given topics, and to do well you're inclined to knowing absolutely everything which makes them exam-like. Nonetheless, Dr. Franceschi doesn't throw curveballs, and the quizzes were the exact same in structure and style as the practice ones he posted. And doing bad on some quizzes won't kill your grade. - homeworks are projects, which were straightforward, and tweaking code examples from class/Canvas will help you a TON. - as with any group assignment: what makes/breaks your grade is your group; at worst, you'll end up doing more work than you intended. As long as the final result follows the rubric, there's nothing to worry about (you won't have to publish your app nor will outsiders be testing it). - midterm/final exams felt very long; exam questions matched practice questions in structure and style. Completing projects is the best way to prepare for the exams, followed by skimming through the code and class examples afterwards. He gave us documentation sheets with some class/functions/interfaces/variables that were on the exam, which guarantees free points if you know how to read. Regrade requests were addressed quickly. - Personal opinions: Dr. Franceschi's lecturing style is monotonous and not the most engaging, but it's far better than a professor who rushes or teaches like everyone already knows everything. He's respectful and clear about the class structure (and any changes to it that come up). Use the recordings to your advantage. I'd rate the course a 4.5/5 if I could. This is a lengthy review, but one that hopefully clears up some misconceptions about the course.

review_text: I may daresay Dr. Dachman-Soled might be one of the better, if not best, crypto professors, especially if you're interested in moving forward with cryptography in any aspect. Her expertise lies very solidly in the domain of the subject, and she emphasizes a lot of the theoretical games that any good cryptographer should be considering when creating a cryptographic algorithm, such as CPA or MacForge. The importance of this can't be understated; from a practical standpoint, it's true that cryptographic algorithms tend to stay pretty constant thanks to NIST standards and cryptographic libraries, but if you're interested in crypto research, these are ideas that are foundational to the subject that even published crypto papers get wrong. She's also one of the few crypto profs that goes over post-quantum crypto, which we're slowly (very, very, very slowly) migrating towards, meaning that if you're interested at all in the future of crypto algorithms, you should absolutely take 456 with her. I enjoyed the subject immensely. The B I got was mostly thanks to me skill-issuing the statistics (I hate statistics) which is a large part of the analysis done on cryptography, especially in regards to information theory. (I also hate linear algebra, which is what a lot of PQC is.) (I'm not very good at math.) That being said, the class is hard as all hell and I don't recommend it with her if you're looking for something easy. I also wish that she covered more of the applications of the crypto algorithms. It's a bit of a shame that we didn't even go over digital signatures even though they're one of the more common applications of asymmetric crypto. If there was a bit more emphasis on real-world cryptosystems, like multi-party computation systems, encrypted messaging channels, or even more discussion on PKI, that would easily elevate this class from a 4 to a 5. On a side note, loved the website. Lots of bells and whistles.

review_text: I was nervous about taking this class since I don't have any neuroscience background, and physics was a prerequisite for this class, but the content wasn't that bad. I don't think physics even needs to be a prereq since if you needed to know something, Dr. Butts would go over it in class. Dr. Butts was generally good at explaining difficult concepts. Sometimes he tripped up, but he corrected himself and made it clear which explanation was right. He was very approachable and open to answering questions. The lectures were very informative and well-paced. He records lectures. You did have to buy PointSolutions to participate in the clicker questions, but he might get rid of that in future semesters, depending on student feedback. The clicker questions were a good gauge of your understanding of the lecture, but I would have preferred not paying for it. Clickers were graded based on participation and attendance, but there was a little extra credit for correct answers. There are no curves in this class, and it uses the standard grade cutoffs. Grades are based on the following: 1st midterm (15%), 2nd midterm (20%), final exam (30%), worksheets (22%), online quizzes (10%), and clickers (3%). The weekly online quizzes were based on assigned textbook chapters and were multiple-choice. You had 1 hour to complete them, and they ranged from 10-20 questions. If you read the chapter beforehand (or use ctrl+F), you should have no problem with the time limit and getting 100%. In-class worksheets were completed in randomly-assigned groups of 4, open note, and lasted 1 lecture period. The worksheets were hard, and my group always asked the TAs to help check our answers. The TAs were also very helpful in understanding how to answer the questions. Often, we would be working right up until class ended. They are graded leniently, so as long as your answer is somewhat right, you should get in the A range. The 1st worksheet also had an extra credit question. There were 5 worksheets total, but Dr. Butts said he could change the number for future classes based on student feedback. The answer keys for the worksheets were posted before exams, so we could use them to study. I felt like all the exams were fair and based on the content covered in the class. Dr. Butts said that content covered in the textbook but not covered in lecture could still be on the exams, but he never included them on our exams. The midterms were a mix of multiple choice (around 10 questions) and free response. Some of the multiple-choice questions were taken straight from the online quizzes. The free-response portion included matching, short-answer, long-answer, and drawing graphs. The review questions and worksheets were helpful for studying for the free-response section, but he didn't post an answer key for the review questions. Instead, they were held like a discussion board where multiple students could comment an answer and correct each other, with Dr. Butts providing feedback. If you wanted definitive answers to the review questions, you had to attend either office hours or the exam review session. The exam review sessions were just big office hours held before each exam, but they were helpful for hearing what questions other students asked to double-check your knowledge. The final was split into a comprehensive portion and the last third of the class content. The questions were the same format as the midterms, but it was longer and had proportionally more free-response questions. I didn't feel pressed for time on any of the exams, but I wouldn't recommend spending too much time on any question since some of the free-response questions were lengthy. I studied for the exams by reviewing the lecture recordings and my notes, completing the review questions, going over the worksheet answer keys and quizzes, and attending the exam review session for last-minute questions. Focus more on understanding concepts and the reasons why something happens rather than just memorizing. This wasn't a class to slack off in, but getting an A was completely doable with some effort.

review_text: MATH430 with Dr. Conway is one of my favorite classes I've taken. This is coming from someone who only took MATH461 last semester, whose only experience with proofs were CMSC250 and CMSC351, and who generally had only a passing interest in mathematics before taking this class, as I'm an engineer first and foremost. I mostly took this class because I had a passing interest in non-Euclidean geometry for several years, and I thought it would help me learn how to think for the proof-based math class I needed for the math minor, which I added this summer for personal reasons. While I can't say for sure whether the latter was fulfilled, as I still generally struggle with thinking like a mathematician in the way many of my classmates have probably been doing for years, I can say that this class was the perfect gateway for me to really start caring about mathematics. I really like Dr. Conway as a lecturer. Particularly for MATH430, he knows the subject extremely well, and since the class is an elective primarily intended for math students, he can easily tailor the lectures and content accordingly. Lectures can be a bit quick, but he posts lecture notes and recordings. He posted the ELMS page about a month before the class started, and I attempted to do the homework before the class started. I failed at this, but going to class helped me a lot with figuring out how to do them and knowing what he expected from our submissions. We covered a variety of topics, but the main ones were straightedge and compass constructions, Hilbert's axioms, finite and infinite projective geometries, isometries, and hyperbolic geometry. They might seem mundane just listing them out, and Euclidean geometry in particular is something I really didn't care about before coming into this class. However, and I don't really understand why, but I enjoyed everything we covered. Nothing in this class was nearly as mundane as everything in my high school geometry class, for example. The grade is split up between 20% homework, 25% for 2 midterms, and 30% for a final project (10% presentation, 20% written). For each homework, we were given a couple problems and were assigned a few of them to turn in (usually the easier ones, but there were some tricky problems here and there). I spent many hours on these, particularly homeworks 4 and 5, but that's just me being unable to see the line of reasoning for proofs. For most people taking this class, these should be pretty easy, as even I scored nearly 100% on all of them. Midterm 1 was also pretty easy in my case, but I think Dr. Conway may have gone a bit easy on grading that one. I personally don't feel my answers for the first two questions were really well-formed, as 50 minutes turns out to be not enough time for me to properly think about problems, but I still somehow got above the median, which was 38.5/40. Midterm 2 was not my greatest moment to put it lightly, as I didn't prepare for it nearly as much as I needed to, and November was generally not my month. The final project was very interesting, as we needed to write on and present a topic of our choosing, as long as we could find a good relation between our topic and geometry beyond the scope of the class. We had a variety of topics in our class, and Dr. Conway provides a list of suggestions to help choose a topic. There are deadlines for a project proposal and written draft weeks before presentations start to keep us from doing it all in the last minute, which is appreciated. As for something I wasn't a huge fan of, it was our required textbook. Dr. Conway mentioned several times that our required textbook (The Four Pillars of Geometry by John Stillwell) is below the level of our class, which I tend to agree with. It's a fine textbook for the Euclidean geometry section of the course, but it seems to just cover the baseline of what we need for non-Euclidean geometries in the last section of the book, and isn't really a proper overview. We didn't even use the book for Hilbert's axioms. The problems in it are fairly easy all things considered, but particularly for non-Euclidean geometry, they aren't representative of what we'd see on exams. Meanwhile, they were the majority of required problems in the last two homeworks. This was evidently not a problem for most people in the class, as the class collectively did well on both exams, so my word should be taken with a grain of salt. Overall, I just really liked this class, and I highly recommend anyone with even a passing interest in any topic in this course to take it with Dr. Conway. It's not especially difficult, and the final project alone pretty much guarantees that there is something to take away from the class for most people.

review_text: Physics 132 with Losert is unfortunately, the best way of taking a physics 2 class without having to do calculus. I don’t remember learning much of anything from either 131 or 132, except for basic conceptual information (but any formulas we learned have completely vanished from my head). No matter which Phys132 professor you take, both are fine, and it's really the actual class material and structure that many students have problems with. Exam 1 had continuation of material from Phys131. Losert made it pretty difficult and not similar to any of the practice exams he has posted on the material. That’s fine, though, as the entire class did poor, and he added 10 points to everyone’s score after the exam. There are always areas where you can essentially get free points on the exam too (essay questions) that, if you write anything remotely close to the topic they ask you, you get full points. Exam 2 was also quite difficult, but again, the class got a 10-point raw curve to everyone’s score, so I actually ended up with a 91%, which was pretty good compared to everyone else. Overall, the exams aren’t worth much in the gradebook (only 20% of the class grade was the midterms) so don’t stress too much. They are also very liberal with partial credit, so even if you just write the formula and some work, they try to give you points. Every exam, including the final, allows you a formula sheet. I recommend just making a sheet for exam 1 on 1/3 of the page and adding to it for each exam, so you don’t have to redo it for the final. Weekly Expert TA Homework - 20%, In-Class Midterm Exams (2) - 20%, Final Exam - 20%, TopHat (RQs, Lecture Participation, Quizzes) - 20%, Lab Reports - 12%, Recitation/Lab Participation - 8%. The final was difficult, with a heavy emphasis on what we learned after exam 2 (50% of the material was new). I found it quite challenging again, and I didn’t really come up with a real answer for probably 25% of the problems. I ended up with a 88% on the final so I'm sure I got a ton of partial credit. Expert TA is awful, and unfortunately, in Phys132, it deducts points for incorrect attempts, so be careful about submitting answers. He then went on a tangent about how you should be taking notes, and if you don't understand something, ask your fellow classmate. He claimed that he is teaching for the "average student," but the truth is that the average student would appreciate better organization and more practice. He asked those two students if it would really be worth their time to do 15 questions before the quiz, as if that would be a bad thing. Hell, even if he doesn't give practice problems, you would hope that he gives you homework problems before the quizzes to work through. Nope. One thing that I want to note is that for homeworks, make sure that there are no mistakes before you submit them. Partial credit is sometimes not a concept when your homework is being graded. review_text: Definitely the best professor to take CHEM131 with!! I have friends who took other professors and I can say this with conviction. The bad reviews are fixating on the fact that test averages were pretty low and yeah, 50-60% isn't GREAT. What they're leaving out is that at the end of the year, as long as you had a 50% in the class, you were guaranteed to pass. He also is very clear that even if you're failing the class, as long as you can pass the final exam with at least a C-, you'll pass the class! He implied that this would be hard, but not because the final was especially evil in difficulty. If you've failed the three midterm exams, it's obviously going to take a lot of work to pass the final?? Not many professors have this policy in place at all. The questions on exams are application-based mostly. I wouldn't call them "trick" questions per se, but you definitely cannot get by on just memorizing the equations and looking for keywords, which is what I think a lot of people tried to do. He was very clear about this from the start of the class; you can't just churn out procedural practice problems for this class. His exams rely on a grasp of the actual theory, but it's not like he leaves you to figure this out yourself. The homeworks he assigns (on Pearson for our class), while challenging, are your BEST bet to learning the material. A lot of students in my class used AI to just finish them and get 100% (they are graded for accuracy and all of them add to a midterm grade) but you also get three attempts each. The homework problems are PURPOSEFULLY MORE DIFFICULT THAN THE EXAM QUESTIONS. As long as you can solidly do the homework, you're fine! He was very clear about the difficulty and value of the homeworks as well. He also gives out a practice exam and study guide a week before each exam, which I was fine with (and found to be standard). While the practice exam might be a little (emphasis on a little) easier, I think it was very representative of the types of exam questions. Timing yourself taking it is a very valuable resource. Also, on each study guide, he'll make it clear what we need to memorize and what will be given on the formula sheet! We also get the formula sheet in advance. TL;DR Lascio is a great professor and cares about your success. I did not have to dedicate more than 2-3 hours/week to the homeworks (which I also used to study). This class is not an easy A by any means, but you'll get out of it what you put in. Don't use AI, do the homeworks, listen to what he SAYS, not just what he WRITES, and be friendly with him. He's a cool dude.

review_text: The reviews of Dr. Wang's teaching style and exams are pretty accurate. Regarding the structure of the class, it was two midterms (150 points each) and a final (250 points), with no graded homework, clicker points, or anything else. So, going into the semester, I was definitely worried about that, but he literally tells you everything on the exam during review days. He makes a list of the reaction conditions, mechanisms, synthesis, and theory concepts on the exam. So as long as you study and check off everything on that list, you'll be fine. The actual content on the exams is essentially a copy and paste from the practice exams he gives you (he also gives you keys to the practice exams). Every exam is formatted the same, with concept/theory first, then reaction conditions, then mechanism, and finally synthesis. You're never blindsighted on question format on the exams, so as long as you study what he tells you, do the practice exam, then the exams will feel very familiar. I will say that exams are pretty lengthy (usually around 10-12 pages), but they are 100% doable in the time he gives you (I have 1.5 exam time and I always finished within the regular time given). Dr. Wang himself is very caring for his students. He always answers questions with a smile on his face and makes sure you understand before leaving his office. One note I do have is that he is not very technologically advanced, so sometimes during the lecture, his camera, which projected the paper he wrote on for practice problems, wouldn't always work, and he doesn't notice, so sometimes you just need to accept that you aren't going to be able to write that problem down. But I don't really have anything negative to say other than that this is kind of a teach yourself type of course. review_text: Sri is not the best lecturer. He started the semester by preparing notes before each lecture, but then later started lecturing straight from the textbook. Many times he would forget how to write a proof and spend several minutes rewriting and erasing his work, which made the material confusing. Also, he frequently blocked the board while writing, which is frustrating when taking notes, and his handwriting is sometimes difficult to read. During class he will answer questions but he does not really encourage them; he also does not stay after class to answer questions. The course is also heavily exam based (90%) with HW 10%, two midterms 20% each, and the final is 50%. Exams tend to be 4-5 questions, with a total score of 15 pts per midterm. Sri would claim the exams would contain some computational questions and homework questions, but then exams would end up being almost entirely proofs from the textbook (along with a few definitions). For tests, I would recommend studying the textbook and memorizing proofs/definitions from the chapters rather than reviewing HW's. Also, given the small number of questions and low point total, if you forgot a specific textbook proof you could lose a fairly significant amount of points. The final exam seemed slightly easier, with more definitions and one challenge problem. There was a good curve at the end of the class though. He grades exams pretty quickly but there is no feedback. HW's were graded half for completion and half on one randomly chosen problem, so there was feedback for only one problem. By the end of the course only 4 of the total 8 HWs were graded. Overall, I think this class would be more informative and easier with another professor. This was his first semester teaching at UMD though. If you are good at memorizing/writing proofs then you will likely do fine in his class, especially given the curve.

You learn some useful things, but for a class, it's just pretty pointless when you could very easily learn relevant info yourself before taking quantum. In other words, I think there isn't enough useful info in this course to have it as a separate course entirely, and I feel that it was a bit too much of a waste. While at the time of writing this I haven't taken quantum yet, I think you could learn all the quantum stuff in quantum, i.e. you don't need this course to get introduced to quantum. The quantum stuff you go over is pretty basic, and honestly you learn techniques for solving very simple problems moreso than concepts, which I feel is more important. I appreciated that she gave practice exams, which definitely helped you prepare for each exam. There were also exam review sessions held by the TAs, which were relatively useful. Finally there are homework and exam corrections, which just aren't needed for a course like this, but still that's a good thing (though I heard you have to write a lot even for simple mistakes that don't require such explanations because there isn't much to reflect on). Overall, you shouldn't have too much difficulty with this class. Just review HWs and do the practice exam for each exam and you'll be fine. Honestly, I think people subconsciously think she's an awesome teacher because this class is so easy compared to other classes they've taken.. don't let that fool you too.

review_text: 3.5 stars, genuinely she isn't as bad as people say. Honestly, I feel her reviews are a little too harsh. Since I didn’t understand anything in this class, I ditched and went to lunch instead and ate fire munch. When I had to miss class for a few days, he was actually very nice in office hours and literally spent like two hours going through the lectures with me. Cons: Mentioned this before, but I didn’t grasp what he taught in lecture since he would drone on and on and often lose his train of thought, so I basically spent the whole semester self-teaching with the help of the holy ChatGPT Plus. Exams were a doozy. They include a definition section, a math problem or two, sometimes a mechanism, short answers, and long answers. But you really have no idea going in which topics are going to be emphasized, so you have to know hundreds of slides’ worth of lecture material cold. It felt like ChatGPT-generated multiple-choice nonsense. I genuinely don’t know how we were supposed to study for it because it was based on random stuff. How to Do Well: Literally put every lecture into ChatGPT and go through each topic to make sure you really understand it. Keep up with lectures, especially if you need to self-teach like I did. For exams, make flashcards with definitions for vocab words and know them cold. Obviously I used Madam Chat to help me make study guides. For each lecture, I had sections for vocabulary, big ideas/concepts, math, and mechanisms. Study according to the format of the exams. For STEM students, writing out concepts precisely is harder than it seems, so practice actually writing definitions and key ideas. Active studying is crucial. As you’re studying, try to predict what he might ask for the long-answer essay and make sure you know it cold and can explain it clearly. Highly recommend reviewing a summary of the material with friends before the exam and trying to figure out what’s high-yield. What I Should Have Done: In genetics, you learn a lot of processes with many steps. I spent way too much time memorizing those, but he usually didn’t test on them. Be very mindful of what you’re devoting your study time to. Since I didn’t go to lecture much, I wish I had gone to office hours more. I think that would’ve helped me get a better sense of what was going to be tested, because I felt pretty blind going into exams. Overall: Tackle the material head-on, make sure you truly understand it, and don’t fall behind. When studying, physically write out definitions and high-yield material so you’re prepared to do that on the exam. Good luck!
